content: We do not account for the long-term benefits of diagnosing and curing individuals with Hepatitis C Virus (HCV). These benefits include reductions in morbidity and mortality associated with end-stage liver disease, as well as decreased onward transmission of the virus. In this preliminary study, it was not feasible to incorporate a model of disease progression and HCV transmission. Future research on HCV self-testing (HCVST) should present outcomes in terms of cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) or disability-adjusted life year (DALY). This approach would enable decision-makers to compare the cost-effectiveness of HCVST with other interventions. Currently, the cost per diagnosis and cost per cure of HCVST can be compared to alternative strategies aimed at improving linkage to care, as well as to the existing cost per diagnosis in the absence of HCVST. Our findings suggest that introducing HCVST will increase the rates of diagnosis and cure among HCV-infected individuals. However, this will require additional resources compared to the current standard of care testing and treatment pathways.
